Skip to content Mum Talks Meet Ups In-person meet ups for Mums looking to connect with other Mums, feel inspired and learn something new. Connect Mum Talks Meet Ups We host Mum Talks Meet Ups in comfortable, easily-accessible and relaxed venues where babes on knees /buggies are always welcome. You’ll always receive a very warm welcome, a yummy light breakfast, and loads of hot coffee. While enjoying breakfast, you’ll listen to amazing speakers and we guarantee when you leave you will feel uplifted and rejuvenated. You can come solo or with friends, and join like-minded mums in a relaxed environment where you can connect, be inspired, feel empowered and – most importantly – know you are not alone when navigating the maze of motherhood. Skip to content Bump Talks Bump Talks is an online event for expectant mums-to-be, a special event all about you to help you carve out some me-time during this exciting (but sometimes tiring!) period. A GREAT EXPERIENCE FOR EXPECTANT MOTHERS Bump Talks Consisting of a combination of a gentle yoga class (recommended from 14 weeks), relaxing meditation and an empowering talk, Bump Talks will focus on what you need as you transition to being a mum for the first time … or for the fifth time! We really hope you can join us and take this time out for yourself to relax, recharge and learn. Skip to content About Us First and foremost, Mum Talks is a community. Our objective is to provide a safe, supportive and empowering network for women in Ireland who are also mums. Supporting, inspiring and empowering women through their journey of motherhood About Us What and Why? Mum Talks is an events company that supports, inspires, and empowers women through their journey of motherhood with in-person and online meet-ups, events, talks, and workshops. Mum Talks provides a safe, and supportive network for mums so they know they’re not alone, can learn from experts and check in with others who are going through the same experience and reality of motherhood. Mum Talks was created eight years ago. Inspired by her own experiences of early motherhood, Lucy O’Driscoll Edge realised that while there were countless activities centred on the baby, very little existed to truly support the mum herself and acknowledge the huge transition a woman goes through when she becomes a mother. Lucy O'Driscoll Edge Founder & MD Lucy is the founder of Mum Talks, a community dedicated to supporting and connecting mothers. Passionate about helping women navigate motherhood, she has spent over nine years bringing mums together through events and conversations. Lucy has interviewed more than 100 experts and speakers who work with mothers and families, and loves creating spaces where women feel supported, informed, and connected. I’ve been working in the IT sector for more than a decade here in Ireland. I love communicating, creativity and sharing my experience of living in a different culture as a first-time mom. I’d like to be by your side, celebrating the messy, beautiful chaos of motherhood without forgetting ourselves. my instagram for my personal blog is @askgelica Donna Ward Location: Longford Donna, mum to 2 amazing girls. Donna has worked in childcare since 1999 and is a qualified Montessori educator, has a BA Hons in early childhood education and care and is the manager of school age childcare setting in Longford. Donna is the founder of Ickle Minds which provides sensory and messy play classes and workshops for children from 6mths onwards. Karen Prunty Location: South Dublin Karen Prunty is a Paediatric Nurse with 14 years of experience, a mum of four, and founder of Little Roo. Tracy is also the author of best selling-memoir “Raising Resilience” and she’s also a passionate advocate for Maternal Mental Health. As one of her sons, Freddie, also has Down Syndrome she prides herself on being an advocate for him, and the Down Syndrome community also. BOOK TICKETS Mum Talks is a fantastic opportunity for mums to connect, share experiences, and learn from each other. Whether you’re a new mum or a seasoned pro , this event is all about supporting one another on this motherhood journey. At Mum Talks, you’ll hear inspiring stories from other mums, gain valuable insights, and get practical tips on various topics. Plus, there will be plenty of time to mingle, make new friends , and enjoy some well-deserved time focused on you. So, grab your mum friends or come by yourself and join us for a morning filled with laughter, learning, and connection. Get ready to be inspired and empowered as we navigate the incredible journey of motherhood together! Babies are always welcome! Light breakfast and tea & coffee included in ticket price. Meet Your Host Louise Spencer Stevens I’m Louise, a mum of two and founder of Messy Adventures Ireland, a business built around connection, play and supporting families. I’m passionate about creating spaces where women feel understood, supported and inspired. I am incredibly excited to be a Mum Talks ambassador, helping build a community where mums can share honest experiences, learn from each other and feel less alone while embracing motherhood and pursuing their own dreams. Date & Time 18 Nov 2026 10:00 - 12:00 Dublin AVOCA, Malahide BOOK TICKETS Speakers Alison O'Driscoll Alison O’Driscoll is a Dublin-based Skin & Makeup Educator and qualified makeup artist with a passion for helping women feel confident in their own skin. Particularly passionate about supporting busy mums, Alison understands that time is precious and that looking after yourself can often fall to the bottom of the list. Her approach is all about taking the pressure out of beauty, cutting through the overwhelming number of products, steps and trends, and showing you how to make the most of what you already have. Sasha Carroll Sasha is a full-time mum, semi-retired content creator, and recently launched a small interiors and soft furnishings studio in Dublin. After experiencing pregnancy loss and her own fertility challenges, she values honesty and compassion in her work and life. She’s passionate about creating timeless, comforting spaces at home, and encouraging new mums to explore their creativity and pursue something new for themselves. Date & Time 26 Nov 2026 10:30 - 12:30 Wicklow The Pigeon House BOOK TICKETS Speakers Michelle Flynn Michelle Flynn is an IACP-accredited psychotherapist, clinical supervisor, somatic practitioner, trainer and lecturer with over 20 years’ experience in mental health. She is the founder of An Croí Beag Psychotherapy, a growing practice of psychotherapists specialising in perinatal and reproductive mental health. As a trauma specialist, Michelle brings warmth, compassion and a deep understanding of how our experiences can shape both mind and body. She works with both top-down and bottom-up approaches, recognising the important role the nervous system plays in emotional wellbeing, trauma and healing. Her work combines reflection and insight with gentle attention to bodily sensations, emotions and nervous-system responses, helping clients develop greater awareness, regulation and a stronger sense of safety. Michelle has a particular interest in matrescence—the profound emotional, physical, psychological and social transition into motherhood. She understands that becoming a parent can bring joy and connection, while also bringing uncertainty, grief, vulnerability and changes in identity. As a mother of three, Michelle brings personal understanding alongside her professional expertise. She is passionate about supporting women through this vulnerable and extraordinary stage of life, offering a safe and compassionate space for feelings and experiences that may not always be easy to put into words. At the heart of her work is the understanding that motherhood can open parts of us we never knew were there. It can bring us closer to our strengths, our vulnerabilities and the parts of ourselves that need care, too. index.t: The Golden Boy: When Your Brother Is the Favourite Child
index.x:
You know the moment. Your brother walks into the kitchen and the whole room changes. Your mother's face softens, a plate appears in front of him, and someone asks how he's  really  getting on. You've been at the table for an hour. You brought the dessert. You cleared the plates from the starter. Nobody noticed. 

 If you grew up as the sister of a golden boy, you don't need anyone to explain that feeling. You've carried it since you were small: the quiet sense that love in your house was shared out, and your brother got the bigger slice. 

 This piece is for you. It isn't here to bash brothers or to put parents on trial. It's here to say something many women have never heard said out loud:  what you felt was real, it mattered, and you are allowed to name it.  

 
   
   The family table: where so much of this plays out, one plate and one question at a time. 
 

 You are not imagining it 

 Families love to tell the sister she's "too sensitive". But researchers have studied favouritism for decades, and it is not a myth. One long-running study of older mothers by sociologists Karl Pillemer and Jill Suitor found that around seven in ten mothers could name the child they felt closest to. Their grown-up children were even more convinced that a favourite existed. 

 Here's the part that's harder to hear. In 2025, a large review of research on favouritism, covering more than 19,000 people, found that the children who got less favourable treatment tended to have poorer mental health and more strained family relationships. That review also found that, on average, parents say they slightly favour daughters. So when it's the son who gets the gold star in your family, it often isn't about who is easier to love. It's about what each child is  expected  to be. 

 Being the favourite and being let off aren't the same thing, and in many families they get tangled up. The boy is let off. The girl is relied on. Over the years, being relied on starts to feel a lot like being overlooked. 

 
   He was the one they worried about. I was the one they leaned on. It took me thirty years to realise those aren't the same as being loved. 
 

 How it shows up 

 Favouritism is rarely one big moment. It's a thousand small ones that settle into a pattern. If you're a sister, some of these may sting with recognition: 

 
    The chores gap.  You set the table, minded the younger ones and did the washing up. He was "out with the lads" or "studying", and somehow that counted. 
    The excuses.  When he lashed out it was "boys will be boys". When you did, you were "dramatic", "hormonal" or "a madam". 
    The spotlight.  His match, his exams, his new job, his girlfriend: big news. Your degree, your promotion, your engagement: "lovely, pet", and back to talking about him. 
    The money and the freedom.  He got the car, the later curfew, the help with the deposit. You got told to be sensible. 
    The forgiveness.  He could disappear for weeks and get a hero's welcome. Miss one Sunday dinner and you heard about it for months. 
    The caring.  And later, when your parents need looking after, everyone simply assumes it'll be you. The same research found that most mothers already had one child in mind as their future carer. Ask the sisters of golden boys who that usually is. 
 

 
   
    The invisible daughter.  Many women describe it this way: always in the room, but never quite the reason it lit up. 
 

 What it does to a girl, and to the woman she becomes 

 Children are brilliant at reading the room, but they always get the explanation wrong. A little girl doesn't think  "my parents have unexamined beliefs about gender."  She thinks  "there must be something wrong with me."  

 Then she gets to work fixing it. That's why so many sisters of golden boys grow into the same kind of woman: 

 
    The over-achiever,  still chasing an A+ from someone who never marks her paper. 
    The fixer,  who organises every birthday, every Christmas and every crisis, and fee
